opus-5.5.text:
I think the line is actually blurrier than people want it to be, and I try to be honest with myself about that. When I post about a paper on X, part of me obviously wants people to see it. Nobody spends six months or a year on a project and then hopes no one reads it. So I don't pretend there's zero self-interest involved.

But the test I use is roughly this: am I trying to help someone understand something, or am I trying to make them believe something about me? If I'm explaining why we made a design choice, what surprised us, what didn't work, where the limitations are, that feels like sharing. It's continuing the conversation that the paper started. If I find myself drafting a thread that's mostly superlatives, "state of the art," "game-changer," cherry-picked figures, and I'm thinking more about how many likes it gets than whether someone in the field will learn from it, that's when I know I've drifted into promotion.

Another thing I pay attention to is credit. Most of the work I post about is really driven by students and collaborators. If the post makes it look like it's my idea or my achievement, that's a red flag. I'd much rather the thread make the first author visible, because for a PhD student, that visibility genuinely matters for their career, while for me it matters much less at this point.

And honestly, I've also learned to be comfortable posting things that aren't flattering: negative results, critiques of trends I think are overhyped, even disagreements with people I respect. Fame-seeking tends to push you toward saying what's popular. Sharing research, in the real sense, sometimes means saying something unpopular and accepting that it won't go viral.

So I'd say it's less about the act of posting and more about the intent and the content. The platform is just a tool. Research has always needed communication, and X is one of the channels now, whether we like it or not. The question is whether you use it to make the science clearer or just to make yourself louder.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes sharing research to help people understand the work from promotion focused on shaping perceptions of the speaker or gaining attention for themself.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, honestly, because the line is blurry and I don't think anyone who posts regularly can claim to be totally pure about it.

The way I try to think about it is: who is the post for? When I share a paper, I ask myself whether the content would be useful to someone even if they never cited me or followed me. If I'm explaining what the idea actually is, what surprised us, what didn't work, what the limitations are, then that's sharing. If I'm just saying "new SOTA, huge jump, thread below" with a bunch of fire emojis, that's marketing, and I try to catch myself.

There's also a very practical reason to share. The field moves incredibly fast now. If you publish a paper and don't talk about it, it can genuinely disappear within a week. So for a student who worked on something for a year, posting about it isn't vanity, it's almost a responsibility of the advisor. I actually feel more comfortable promoting my students' work than my own, because the motivation is clearer to me.

But I'll admit the incentives are real. Attention translates into citations, into recruiting, into funding. You'd be lying if you said that doesn't matter. What I try to do is keep a few habits. I share negative results and things I got wrong, not just wins. I engage with other people's work as much as my own. And I try to write posts the way I'd explain the idea to a colleague over coffee, not the way a press release would.

The simplest test for me is: would I be embarrassed if a researcher I really respect read this post? If the answer is yes, it's probably promotion rather than sharing.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts useful explanations of the research with attention-seeking marketing, and acknowledges fame-related incentives such as attention, citations, recruiting, and funding.

astra-6.text:
For me, the distinction is what you want people to pay attention to. Are you trying to get people interested in an idea, or are you trying to get people interested in you? Of course, those two things aren’t completely separable. When you share good research, you build a reputation, and that’s fine.

I think the useful test is whether the post gives people something beyond an announcement. Can they understand the problem, what you found, and where the limitations are? Can they disagree with you and have a discussion? That’s the kind of sharing I value.

But I wouldn’t pretend that I’m immune to wanting recognition. You put a lot of effort into a project, and you want people to notice it. The important thing is not to let that desire start determining which problems you work on or how strongly you present your conclusions.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes drawing attention to an idea from drawing attention to oneself, and says that sharing research can build a reputation without making fame the aim.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the distinction is really about what you want people to take away. Are you helping them understand an idea, or are you mainly trying to get attention for yourself? Of course, those motivations can coexist. You do good work, you want people to see it, and that’s perfectly reasonable.

I think a useful test is whether you’re willing to discuss the limitations as openly as the results. Can you explain what worked, what didn’t, and how it connects to other people’s work? Then sharing becomes part of the research process. People can question it, and you can learn something.

On X, it’s easy to start optimizing for the reaction. A strong claim gets attention, and then you feel pressure to make the next claim even stronger. I think you have to keep asking yourself: am I making this clearer, or just making it sound bigger?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts helping people understand the research with seeking attention for oneself, and says sharing work so people can see it is reasonable.
